description: CS students from ECU, working on the challenge about finding places on Earth that match the ground on the Moon and Mars. We can handle the code. What we cannot fake is the geology, so if you study rocks, deserts, or remote sensing, we want you. Message us and we will show you what we have.
summary: Planetary Twin Finder finds the places on Earth whose ground best matches the sites NASA has proposed for landing humans on Mars and the Moon. Astronauts and rovers rehearse at a handful of Earth analogs, chosen mostly by field experience. We compared the whole dry planet instead. Every patch of ground on Earth, Mars and the Moon is described with the same four numbers (slope, roughness, relief and brightness) at the same 463 m pixel size as NASA's Mars elevation map. Earth ground with plants, water or ice is removed, and each NASA site gets a ranked, explained list of its closest Earth twins. In a blind test, without being told where NASA trains, 92.5% of our Mars matches landed in the Atacama Desert and Death Valley, NASA's best-known analogs. The method also found new ones: Jezero crater's closest twin, #1 of 148,925 dry places in Africa and the Americas, is in Egypt's Eastern Desert. Mission planners, field-test teams and students can use the website to find nearer, cheaper and more varied places to rehearse for the Moon and Mars.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

The website has two parts. A scroll story explains the problem, the method and the results. The Twin Finder lets anyone pick one of NASA's 47 proposed landing sites (the 38 candidate human Exploration Zones on Mars and the nine Artemis III candidate regions at the lunar south pole) and see its 25 closest twins on Earth on a satellite map. Each twin card shows its score, its rank among all dry places on Earth and within its continent, how close each of the four features is, a side-by-side shaded relief of the target and the twin, what Earth cannot copy (for the Moon, Diviner temperatures and ice-stability shares), and links to Google Maps, NASA Worldview and the Copernicus Browser. An "Ask the analyst" panel answers questions about the result on screen, using only our data.

HOW TO TRY IT

Open https://duplicaa.vercel.app, click "Launch the Twin Finder", keep Mars and Jezero selected, and open twin #1 (Egypt). Then switch to the Moon and pick any Artemis region.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Every world is cut into tiles about 9.26 km across (20 x 20 pixels of 463 m, the resolution of NASA's MOLA map of Mars). Earth and Moon elevation are averaged down to the same pixel size, so all three worlds are measured the same way.

2. Each tile gets four numbers: mean slope, slope spread (roughness), relief (highest minus lowest point) and albedo (brightness).

3. On Earth, a tile is kept only if it could look like Mars: median NDVI below 0.15 (no plants), under 5% permanent water, and under 50% permanent snow and ice. That leaves 148,925 dry tiles in Africa and the Americas south of 50 N (130,060 in Africa).

4. Features are standardized together, and each Earth tile's distance to a NASA site is its mean distance to the site's 10 nearest tiles. The score is 100 x exp(-distance / 0.4), so 100 is a perfect match. Twins in a list are at least 25 km apart.

5. The Moon is matched on terrain only, with its own scaler. Its scores (best 5 to 33) are much lower than Mars scores (best 63 to 98), because the lunar south pole is rougher than almost any dry land, so the site shows ranks rather than scores for the Moon.

HOW WE KNOW IT WORKS

We tested the method blind. Without telling it where NASA trains, 92.5% of its Mars matches fell in the Atacama Desert and Death Valley; a wet farmland control box (the Nile Delta) got 7.5%, and those were desert tiles east of Cairo, not farmland. We kept the failures too: adding heat as a feature dropped the result to 84.3%, and ranking by percentiles within each world let the farmland control rise to 28.3%. Known answers check the terrain code: Shackleton crater comes out 4.06 km deep (published 4.2 km).

BENEFITS

Mission teams can shortlist new analog sites from data, then visit only the best ones. Countries without a famous analog can find their own: Egypt's Eastern Desert is the closest twin of Jezero crater, where Perseverance landed. Every result is explained feature by feature, and every limit is stated.

WHAT WORKS NOW AND LIMITS

Working now: the full website, all 47 NASA sites, 25 twins each, the Egypt tab and the analyst. Limits: matching uses terrain shape and brightness at about 460 m (no rock chemistry, no temperature, no boulders); the Earth grid covers Africa and the Americas south of 50 N so far; the Moon has no brightness feature yet. Results are a ranked shortlist, not a substitute for visiting a site.

NEXT

Cover the rest of the world, add Moon brightness (LOLA albedo), add an image-based engine, and a reverse mode that finds the nearest good twin to any city.

TOOLS

Python 3.11 (rasterio, GDAL, GeoPandas, NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib, pytest), Google Earth Engine, JavaScript with Vite, three.js, MapLibre GL JS, GSAP and Lenis, Google Gemini for the analyst, hosted on Vercel.
